stem.text: The function f is continuous for all real x and differentiable for all x except \( x = 5 \), where its graph has a corner. Selected values of f are given in the table. Does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee a value c, with \( 1 < c < 9 \), such that \( f'(c) = - \frac{1}{4} \)? Justify the answer.

answer_key.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(9) - f(1)}{9 - 1} = - \frac{1}{4} \), f is not differentiable at \( x = 5 \), which lies in \( (1, 9) \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.

worked_solution.text: The average rate of change of f over \( \left[1, 9\right] \) is \( \frac{f(9) - f(1)}{9 - 1} = \frac{10 - 12}{8} = - \frac{1}{4} \).

The Mean Value Theorem needs f continuous on \( \left[1, 9\right] \) and differentiable on \( (1, 9) \), but f is not differentiable at \( x = 5 \), which lies in \( (1, 9) \). The theorem does not apply, and no other fact given forces \( f'(c) = - \frac{1}{4} \) anywhere in the interval, so the answer is no.
worked_solution.rule_named: hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(9) - f(1)}{9 - 1} = - \frac{1}{4} \), the Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a c, with f taken to be differentiable on \( (1, 9) \).
options.derivation: the Mean Value Theorem applied without checking its hypotheses, which fail at x = 5

Yes. Since \( \frac{f(9) - f(1)}{9 - 1} = - \frac{1}{4} \), there is a c with \( 1 < c < 9 \) and \( f'(c) = - \frac{1}{4} \), because an average rate of change is always reached by the derivative.
